text: In the last lesson you inserted one row at a time. Here you'll insert several rows with a single INSERT statement by listing multiple value tuples.

Add more parenthesized tuples after VALUES, separated by commas, to insert many rows at once. The column list is written only once, right after the table name, and every tuple that follows is matched to it by position, just like a single-row insert.

Tuples are separated by commas, with no comma after the last one and none before the first. Get this wrong — a missing comma, or an extra trailing comma — and SQL Server rejects the entire statement as a syntax error before any row is inserted.

Three single-row inserts and one three-row insert produce the same final data, but they aren't equally efficient. A multi-row VALUES list is parsed, compiled, and logged as one operation, which is noticeably faster than repeating the round trip for every row.

A multi-row insert is still all-or-nothing. If any one tuple violates a constraint, like a missing required ProductName, the entire statement fails and none of the rows are inserted, not just the bad one. That matters when loading external data — validate first, or use smaller batches.
Next, you'll insert rows pulled from a SELECT query instead of typing out literal values.
